title.en: Section 1 - Registering for a Community Art Class
title.zh: 第一部分 - 注册社区艺术课程

sections.passage: A conversation between a new resident, Karen, and the coordinator of a community arts centre, Paul. Karen has recently moved to the area and wants to sign up for art classes. Paul welcomes her and describes the classes available. They offer courses in watercolour painting, oil painting, pottery, and sculpture. The watercolour class runs on Wednesday mornings from 10 AM to 12:30 PM and costs 120 pounds for a ten-week term. The oil painting class is on Thursday evenings from 7 to 9:30 PM and costs 150 pounds for ten weeks, which includes all materials. Karen is interested in both watercolour and pottery. The pottery class is held on Tuesday afternoons from 2 to 4 PM and costs 135 pounds for ten weeks, plus a 20 pounds materials fee. Paul explains that all classes are taught by professional artists. The watercolour tutor is Margaret Davies, who has exhibited her work internationally and has over twenty years of teaching experience. The pottery class is led by James Okoro, a ceramic artist who trained at the Royal College of Art. Karen asks about class sizes and learns that each class has a maximum of fifteen students. Paul mentions that there is a 10 percent discount for students who enroll in more than one class, and a 15 percent discount for senior citizens over 65. Karen, who is 45, decides to enroll in both the watercolour and pottery classes, taking advantage of the multi-class discount. She asks about the start date and Paul confirms that the new term begins on Monday the 9th of September. Karen fills in a registration form and pays by debit card. Paul gives her a list of what to bring to the first class and mentions that the centre also hosts a student exhibition at the end of each term, which is open to the public and free to attend.

title.en: Section 2 - Information Talk about a Recycling Scheme
title.zh: 第二部分 - 关于回收计划的信息说明

sections.passage: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information session about our new recycling scheme. My name is Rachel Green, and I'm the environmental officer for Greenfield Borough Council. I'm here to explain the changes to our waste collection service that will come into effect from the 1st of October. First, some background. Currently, our borough has one of the lowest recycling rates in the country, at just 32 percent. Our target is to reach 50 percent within three years, and the new scheme is designed to help us achieve this. Under the new system, waste will be collected in four separate categories. The green bin will be for garden waste, including grass cuttings, leaves, and small branches. The blue bin will be for paper, cardboard, glass, and metals. The brown bin will be for food waste, and the black bin will be for everything else that cannot be recycled. Collection days will change for some households. Most areas will have collections on the same day each week, alternating between recyclables one week and non-recyclables the next. Food waste will be collected weekly, and garden waste fortnightly between April and October. The council is providing every household with a kitchen caddy for food waste, along with compostable liners. These liners are essential because ordinary plastic bags are not suitable for the composting process. You can collect your caddy and a roll of liners from any of the borough's libraries or from the council offices from the 15th of September. For those of you with large families, additional bins can be requested free of charge by contacting the waste management team. I should also mention that the council is introducing a charge of 40 pounds per year for garden waste collection. This is an optional service — if you don't want to pay, you can take your garden waste to any of the borough's three recycling centres free of charge. The centres are open seven days a week from 8 AM to 6 PM. Finally, I'd like to remind everyone that contaminated recycling — that is, recyclable items that are dirty or mixed with non-recyclable waste — cannot be processed and ends up in landfill. Please make sure all items are clean and dry before placing them in the recycling bin.

title.en: Section 3 - Discussion about an Archaeology Assignment
title.zh: 第三部分 - 关于考古学作业的讨论

sections.passage: Two students, Daniel and Sophia, are meeting to discuss their upcoming assignment for their Archaeology course. They need to write a 3,000-word report on a topic related to ancient civilizations. Daniel has been researching the Indus Valley Civilization, also known as the Harappan Civilization, which flourished in what is now Pakistan and northwest India from approximately 3300 to 1300 BC. He is fascinated by the sophistication of their urban planning, particularly the city of Mohenjo-daro, which had a grid-like street layout, an advanced drainage system, and standardized brick sizes. Sophia has been studying the Minoan civilization of Crete, which existed from around 3000 to 1400 BC. She is interested in the palace of Knossos, which had multiple stories, elaborate frescoes, and a complex plumbing system. She mentions that the Minoans were one of the first European civilizations to develop writing, using a script called Linear A that has not yet been deciphered. They discuss how to approach the assignment. Their tutor, Professor Harrison, has emphasized the importance of comparing at least two civilizations and analyzing the factors that contributed to their rise and decline. Daniel suggests they could compare the urban planning techniques of both civilizations. Sophia agrees and adds that they should also examine the role of trade in sustaining these civilizations. She has found evidence that the Minoans traded extensively with Egypt, while the Harappan civilization had trade links with Mesopotamia. They decide to divide the work, with Daniel focusing on the Harappan sections and Sophia on the Minoan sections. They plan to meet again on Friday to combine their work. Professor Harrison has asked them to use at least eight academic sources, and Sophia suggests using the JSTOR database to find peer-reviewed articles. The assignment is due on the 15th of October, and they want to have a first draft ready by the 8th.

title.en: Section 4 - Lecture on the Economics of Happiness
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于幸福经济学的讲座

sections.passage: Good afternoon. Today's lecture explores the relationship between economic factors and subjective wellbeing, a field that has come to be known as the economics of happiness. For centuries, economists assumed that increasing wealth would lead to increasing happiness. However, research over the past fifty years has revealed a much more complex picture. The pioneering work in this field was done by the economist Richard Easterlin, who in 1974 published what became known as the Easterlin Paradox. Easterlin found that while richer people within a country tend to be happier than poorer people, countries do not become happier as they become wealthier over time. In other words, beyond a certain threshold of income, additional wealth does not appear to increase average happiness levels. This finding challenged the fundamental assumption of conventional economics that economic growth is the primary route to improved human welfare. More recent research has refined and, to some extent, challenged the Easterlin Paradox. A study by economists Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton, published in 2010, found that emotional wellbeing — that is, the quality of a person's daily emotional experience — increases with income only up to about 75,000 dollars per year in the United States, after which it plateaus. However, they also found that life evaluation — how people rate their overall life satisfaction — continues to rise with income even beyond this threshold. This suggests that while money can buy freedom from the daily stresses of poverty, it cannot buy lasting emotional happiness. The factors that have been consistently shown to correlate with higher levels of happiness include the quality of social relationships, employment status, physical health, and a sense of purpose or meaning in life. A major study by Harvard University, which has tracked the lives of 724 men over more than 80 years, concluded that the quality of close relationships is the single strongest predictor of happiness and longevity. Loneliness, conversely, has been shown to be as damaging to health as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Governments around the world have begun to take these findings seriously. The small Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan famously adopted Gross National Happiness as an alternative to GDP as its primary measure of national progress in 1972. New Zealand became the first developed country to present a wellbeing budget in 2019, allocating spending based on the impact on mental health, child poverty, and social connection rather than purely on economic outcomes. The United Nations has published an annual World Happiness Report since 2012, ranking countries by the happiness of their citizens. The Scandinavian countries — Finland, Denmark, Norway, and Sweden — consistently top these rankings, which researchers attribute to their strong social safety nets, low levels of corruption, high levels of social trust, and generous work-life balance policies.

title.zh: 文章1 - 玻璃制造的历史

sections.passage:
Glass is one of the most versatile and ancient materials known to humanity. Its origins can be traced back to around 3500 BC in Mesopotamia and Egypt, where the earliest known glass objects — small beads and ornaments — were produced. The discovery of glassmaking was likely accidental, occurring when sand mixed with plant ash was exposed to high temperatures in cooking fires or primitive furnaces, producing a translucent, brittle substance that we now recognize as glass.

The first significant advances in glassmaking technology came in the first century BC with the invention of glassblowing in the Syro-Palestinian region. This revolutionary technique involved inflating a blob of molten glass at the end of a blowpipe, allowing craftsmen to create hollow vessels quickly and efficiently. Glassblowing transformed glass from a luxury item affordable only by the wealthy into a more accessible material. The Roman Empire enthusiastically adopted this technology, and Roman glass vessels have been found across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East, testament to the extensive trade networks of the ancient world.

During the medieval period, Venice became the centre of European glassmaking. Venetian glassmakers, known as maestri, developed innovative techniques including cristallo, a remarkably clear glass that resembled rock crystal, and millefiori, a decorative technique involving fused coloured glass canes sliced to reveal flower-like patterns. In 1291, the Venetian government decreed that all glassmakers must relocate to the island of Murano, ostensibly to reduce fire risk in the city but also to control the spread of their closely guarded trade secrets. Murano glassmakers were forbidden from leaving the island on pain of death, though despite these precautions, some eventually escaped and established glassmaking centres in other parts of Europe.

The industrial revolution brought mechanization to glass production. In 1903, Michael Owens invented the first fully automatic bottle-making machine, which could produce 2,500 bottles per day — a feat that would have required an entire team of skilled glassblowers working by hand. Perhaps the most significant breakthrough came in 1959 when Sir Alastair Pilkington invented the float glass process, in which molten glass is floated on a bath of molten tin to produce perfectly flat sheets of glass. This process, still used today, made it possible to produce large sheets of high-quality flat glass cheaply and efficiently, revolutionizing the construction industry and making the glass-curtain-wall skyscrapers that define modern city skylines possible.

Today, glass continues to evolve. Gorilla Glass, developed by Corning, is an extraordinarily thin and damage-resistant glass used in billions of smartphones and tablets worldwide. Self-cleaning glass has a special coating that uses ultraviolet light from the sun to break down organic dirt, which is then washed away by rain. Researchers are also developing bioactive glasses that can bond with human tissue, offering promising applications in medicine for bone repair and tissue regeneration. The story of glass is far from over.

title.zh: 文章2 - 森林如何交流

sections.passage:
Forests are far more complex and interconnected than they appear at first glance. Recent scientific discoveries have revealed that trees communicate with each other through an intricate underground network of fungal threads, sharing nutrients, water, and even warning signals about threats such as insect attacks and disease. This remarkable system, sometimes called the Wood Wide Web, is transforming our understanding of forest ecology and challenging the notion that trees are passive, solitary organisms competing for resources.

The underground network is formed by mycorrhizal fungi, which form symbiotic partnerships with the roots of trees. The fine fungal threads, called hyphae, extend far beyond the reach of a tree's own roots, effectively increasing the tree's ability to absorb water and minerals from the soil by up to a thousandfold. In return, the tree provides the fungi with sugars produced through photosynthesis. This mutual exchange benefits both parties and forms the foundation of forest health.

But the relationship goes far beyond simple nutrient exchange. Research led by Professor Suzanne Simard at the University of British Columbia has demonstrated that trees actively share resources through the fungal network. In a groundbreaking study published in 1997, Simard used radioactive carbon isotopes to track the flow of carbon between trees. She discovered that paper birch trees were transferring carbon to Douglas fir trees through their shared fungal connections, particularly when the firs were shaded and receiving less sunlight. Simard described these resource-sharing relationships using the term 'mother tree' to refer to the oldest, largest trees in a forest, which she found to be the most connected nodes in the underground network, linked to hundreds of other trees.

Further research has shown that trees also use the network to communicate danger. When a tree is attacked by insects or infected by disease, it can send chemical warning signals through the fungal network to neighbouring trees. These neighbours then increase the production of defensive chemicals in their own leaves and bark, making them less palatable to the attackers. A study published in 2013 demonstrated that when tomato plants were infected with a pathogen, they sent chemical signals through shared mycorrhizal networks that triggered defensive responses in nearby uninfected plants.

The implications of these findings are profound for forest management. Traditional forestry practices, such as clear-cutting large areas of forest, can destroy the underground fungal network, weakening the ability of remaining trees to survive and regenerate. Simard's research suggests that retaining mother trees during logging operations is essential for maintaining the health and connectivity of the forest ecosystem. Some forestry companies have begun to adopt these practices, selectively harvesting trees while preserving the oldest and most connected individuals.

However, the picture is not entirely harmonious. Some scientists caution against overstating the cooperative nature of forest ecosystems, pointing out that trees also compete fiercely for light, water, and nutrients. The relationships between trees and fungi are complex, involving both mutual benefit and exploitation. Some plant species, known as mycoheterotrophs, cheat the system by tapping into the fungal network and taking nutrients without providing anything in return. Understanding the full complexity of these interactions remains an active and exciting area of research.

title.en: Passage 3 - The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
title.zh: 文章3 - 人工智能伦理

sections.passage:
As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into every aspect of modern life — from healthcare and education to criminal justice and employment — the ethical questions surrounding its use have become impossible to ignore. While AI offers enormous potential benefits, including more accurate medical diagnoses, more efficient transportation systems, and enhanced scientific research, it also raises profound concerns about fairness, accountability, transparency, and the future of human autonomy.

One of the most pressing ethical issues is algorithmic bias. AI systems learn from data, and if that data reflects historical biases, the AI will reproduce and potentially amplify those biases. A well-known example occurred in 2016 when investigative journalists at ProPublica revealed that an AI system used by US courts to predict the likelihood of defendants reoffending was significantly more likely to incorrectly flag Black defendants as high risk compared to white defendants. The algorithm had been trained on historical criminal justice data that reflected decades of systemic racial bias, and it perpetuated these patterns in its predictions. Similarly, studies have shown that AI-powered hiring tools can discriminate against women and minorities if they are trained on historical hiring data that reflects past discriminatory practices.

The question of accountability poses another significant challenge. When an AI system makes a harmful decision — such as a self-driving car causing an accident, or a medical AI system misdiagnosing a patient — it can be extremely difficult to determine who is responsible. Is it the programmer who wrote the code, the company that deployed the system, the organization that provided the training data, or the user who relied on the AI's recommendation? Current legal frameworks were not designed to handle these questions, and many countries are grappling with how to adapt their laws to the AI era. The European Union's proposed AI Act, which aims to establish a comprehensive regulatory framework for artificial intelligence, represents one of the most ambitious attempts to address these issues.

Privacy is another major concern. AI systems often require vast amounts of personal data to function effectively. Facial recognition technology, for instance, can identify individuals in real time from surveillance camera footage, raising concerns about mass surveillance and the erosion of privacy. In China, a social credit system uses AI to monitor and evaluate the behaviour of citizens, determining their access to services such as travel, education, and banking based on their social score. While proponents argue that such systems improve public safety and social harmony, critics view them as instruments of authoritarian control.

The impact of AI on employment is also a subject of intense debate. A widely cited study by Oxford University in 2013 estimated that 47 percent of jobs in the United States were at high risk of automation within the next two decades. While subsequent research has suggested that the figure may be lower — a 2020 study by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development estimated 14 percent — there is broad consensus that AI will significantly transform the labour market, creating new types of jobs while rendering others obsolete. The question of how to manage this transition, including the potential need for universal basic income and massive retraining programmes, remains one of the most important policy challenges of the 21st century.

options.zh: 它对所有被告完全公平

options.en: It was biased against Black defendants
It was biased in favor of minorities

text.en: What does algorithmic bias result from?

options.en: AI training data reflecting historical biases
options.zh: AI训练数据反映的历史偏见

text.en: When was the ProPublica investigation published?
text.zh: ProPublica的调查是什么时候发表的？

text.en: What is the proposed EU AI Act intended to do?
text.zh: 拟议的欧盟AI法案旨在做什么？

options.en: Ban all AI development in Europe
Establish a comprehensive regulatory framework for AI
options.zh: 为AI建立全面的监管框架

text.en: What does facial recognition technology raise concerns about?
text.zh: 面部识别技术引起了什么担忧？

options.en: Mass surveillance and erosion of privacy
options.zh: 大规模监控和隐私侵蚀

text.en: What does China's social credit system evaluate?
text.zh: 中国的社会信用系统评估什么？

options.en: Citizens' behavior to determine access to services
options.zh: 公民行为以确定服务使用权

text.en: What did the 2013 Oxford study estimate about job automation?
text.zh: 2013年牛津大学研究对工作自动化估计了什么？

options.en: 10 percent of jobs were at risk
25 percent of jobs were at risk
47 percent of jobs were at risk
75 percent of jobs were at risk

text.en: What did the 2020 OECD study estimate?
text.zh: 2020年经合组织研究估计了什么？

text.en: What solution is mentioned for managing the employment transition?
text.zh: 提到了什么解决方案来管理就业转型？

options.en: Universal basic income and retraining programmes
options.zh: 全民基本收入和再培训计划

text.en: Why can AI-powered hiring tools discriminate?
text.zh: 为什么AI驱动的招聘工具可能产生歧视？

options.en: They are programmed to be discriminatory
options.zh: 它们被编程为歧视性的

options.en: They are trained on historically biased hiring data
options.zh: 它们基于历史上有偏见的招聘数据进行训练
它们无法正确处理简历

options.en: They favor candidates with more education
options.zh: 它们偏爱教育程度更高的候选人

text.en: What challenge does the accountability question pose?
text.zh: 问责制问题提出了什么挑战？

options.en: AI systems are too expensive to regulate
It is difficult to determine who is responsible for harmful AI decisions
options.zh: 很难确定谁应对有害的AI决定负责

options.en: AI systems cannot be held accountable
There are too many AI companies to oversee

text.en: What is the broad consensus about AI's impact on employment?
text.zh: 关于AI对就业影响的广泛共识是什么？

options.en: AI will create more jobs than it destroys
options.zh: AI创造的工作将多于其消灭的工作

options.en: AI will significantly transform the labour market
options.zh: AI将显著改变劳动力市场

options.en: AI will have minimal impact on employment
options.zh: AI对就业的影响微乎其微

options.en: AI will eliminate all manual labor jobs
options.zh: AI将消除所有体力劳动工作

text.en: What is described as one of the most important policy challenges?
text.zh: 什么被描述为最重要的政策挑战之一？

prompt.en: The line graph below shows the average monthly temperature in three cities over a year. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
prompt.zh: 下面的折线图显示了三个城市一年中月平均温度。通过选择和报告主要特征来总结信息，并在相关地方进行比较。至少写150个单词。

prompt.en: In many countries, the gap between the rich and the poor is increasing. What problems does this cause, and what solutions can be proposed? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh: 在许多国家，贫富差距正在扩大。这会导致什么问题，可以提出什么解决方案？给出你回答的理由，并包括你自己的知识或经验中任何相关的例子。至少写250个单词。
